To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
PerR is a key regulator for aerotolerance in anaerobic bacteria.

(1) the active form of the peroxide regulator PerR is the one that binds dioxygen; (2) the PerR/Dna complex is disrupted by dioxygen; (3) the PerR response to H2O2 is assisted by dioxygen; and (4) PerR sensing of dioxygen and H2O2 are likely to be physiologically meaningful for anaerobes.

the active form (Fe(II)) of the peroxide regulator PerR reacts with molecular oxygen to form a complex that disrupts the DNA-binding activity of the protein, and this process is likely to be important in the response to air exposure of several anaerobes.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the molecular basis of bacterial resistance to peroxides, which is a major problem for the development of new antibiotics.
the molecular basis of sensing of reactive oxygen species in anaerobes.
a novel mechanism of O2 sensing in the absence of heme, a mechanism that may be important to the survival of pathogenic bacteria in vivo.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
PerR is a sensor for O2 that is able to detect H2O2.
PerR is a sensor of H2O(2) and that the presence of dioxygen assists PerR in sensing H(2)O(2) in anaerobes.
, under anaerobic conditions, the PerR regulon is repressed, but the PerR protein is not inactive.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the PerR system is an O2-dependent H2O2 sensor that may play a role in aerotolerance in strict anaerobics.
PerR, which is a transcriptional repressor, can be converted into an activator of gene expression by the presence of molecular oxygen.
PerR, a regulator that is involved in the resistance to peroxides, also acts as a sensor of oxygen and H2O2 in anaerobes.
The main takeaway from our work is that
PerR, which is a peroxide sensor, is also a dioxygen sensor.
the PerR protein is a sensor of both oxygen and peroxide and that the sensing mechanism is likely different from that of HpxR and DprA.
the presence of molecular oxygen is likely to be important in the regulation of PerR-dependent gene expression, and this may be of relevance in the context of the virulence of pathogenic bacteria.
